8.text: PRESENT STATE. — Of the three Chukchee missionaries who were on the

9.text: Kolyma in the nineties of the nineteenth century, during my stay there, one,

10.text: Father Victor (see Plate XXXV, Fig. 2), lived constantly in Nishne-Kolymsk.

11.text: He was the missionary for the Maritime Chukchee, and the head of the

12.text: mission. The chief interest of his life lay in dog raising. He spent all his

13.text: salary on his team, though he could not drive it himself, but kept a special

14.text: driver. As to the interests of the mission, year after year he made preparations

15.text: for some far-off trip, but somehow every year his plans were frustrated. The

16.text: nearest Maritime Chukchee lived on Cape Erri, and at one time a voyage

17.text: to Cape Erri was actually undertaken by him. He found the people in the

18.text: first Chukchee settlement all murdered, and fled back, horror-stricken. I have

19.text: referred to this episode before. Father Victor knew nothing of the Chukchee

20.text: language, or even of the trade jargon.¹

21.text: Father Venedict was the missionary for the western Reindeer Chukchee.

22.text: He lived, as already mentioned, on the western tundra, in a Yakut settlement,

23.text: Sen-quel. Some of the Reindeer Chukchee of the western tundra would

24.text: occasionally come to his place, and he would try to have intercourse with

25.text: them. For this purpose he had to employ two interpreters. One translated

26.text: from Russian into Yakut. All the Russian creoles from the Middle Kolyma

27.text: can do as much. The other interpreter, usually one of the Yukaghir of the

28.text: tundra who wander thereabouts, translated from Yakut into Chukchee. Through

29.text: this double medium Father Venedict had to preach the Gospel to his Reindeer

30.text: Chukchee flock. One may imagine the success he would have in this enter-

31.text: prise. His stay at Sen-quel was interrupted by an unpleasant official investi-

32.text: gation concerning a certain kettle that was spirited away from one of his

33.text: neighbors. The accusation was not proved, and so came to nought. After

34.text: that, however, he did not care to stay at Sen-quel. Father Venedict was a

35.text: man of many eccentricities. He was said to have come from Russia to Yakutsk

36.text: on foot. While on the Kolyma, he wrote several letters to the civil and

37.text: spiritual authorities, denouncing other priests of the Kolyma, and also various

38.text: laymen. His denunciations were quite groundless, and without result. He

39.text: also boasted aloud of having promised the Bishop of Yakutsk, that, unlike

40.text: the other missionaries, he would make the rounds through all the villages

41.text: and camps of the Chukchee, and bring them all to holy baptism. For this

42.text: purpose he received from the bishop two thousand rubles. His enmity towards
